analysis.one_liner: Ends the entire federal income, corporate, and estate tax code with no replacement written.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in March 1999, and it never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have abolished nearly every federal tax — income taxes on people and businesses, the estate tax, and excise taxes — after December 31, 2003. It would have kept only payroll taxes (the ones that fund Social Security and Medicare and are deducted from paychecks). It did not write a replacement tax system; it just listed principles a future one should follow, and set a July 4, 2003 deadline for Congress to approve one. No replacement was ever part of the bill, so if it had passed and nothing replaced the code, the government would have lost nearly all of its funding source.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners would be the households and businesses that pay the most income tax — high earners and large estates — since their main taxes would disappear while the payroll taxes that fall most heavily on working people would continue unchanged. Anyone benefiting from federal programs funded by income taxes would lose unless a replacement was enacted on time.

how_it_helps.text: It would end all income, corporate, estate, gift, and excise taxes under the Internal Revenue Code for taxable years after December 31, 2003.

It keeps the self-employment tax and the payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act and Railroad Retirement Tax Act in place, so Social Security and Medicare payroll funding would continue.

It declares that any replacement system should be simple, apply a low rate to all Americans, provide tax relief for working Americans, eliminate the bias against savings and investment, and not penalize marriage or families, and should be approved by Congress by July 4, 2003.

analysis.who_pays: With no replacement system written into the bill, the cost would fall on anyone who relies on federal programs funded by income taxes — defense, roads, schools, veterans' care, and safety-net programs — since only payroll-tax-funded programs would keep their dedicated money. If Congress passed a replacement on time, the burden would depend entirely on that future design, which the bill leaves open. Working people would keep paying payroll taxes either way.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federally funded programs

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the tax code without writing a replacement, so if no new system were approved by the July 4, 2003 deadline it sets, the federal government would have almost no revenue except payroll taxes — roughly the entire non-Social-Security budget would be unfunded.

The payroll taxes the bill preserves are the ones that take the largest share of a working family's paycheck, while the taxes it abolishes — income and estate taxes — fall mostly on higher incomes, so the change is worth far more to the wealthy than to ordinary workers.
A hard end date for the entire tax code, years before a replacement existed, would create enormous uncertainty for households, businesses, and financial markets during the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a statement of principle more than a working law: it set a sunset date for the tax code and listed eight goals for a future system but never drafted that system. The benefit it promises is a simpler, fairer tax code with lower rates, but the only concrete thing it does is delete nearly all federal revenue on a fixed date, with a deadline for a replacement that Congress might miss. The payroll taxes it keeps are the ones ordinary workers pay most heavily, while the income and estate taxes it ends weigh most on the wealthy. As a negotiating or messaging device it had value; as an actual change to the tax system it was high-risk and unworkable on its own terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Hutchinson introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on March 16, 1999, joined by 20 Republican cosponsors named at introduction.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
The full action history shows no further action — no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor vote — before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No taxpayer group gained, because the bill never came close to a vote and the existing tax code continued unchanged. The clearest beneficiary of the outcome was the existing federal revenue system itself, which kept funding programs the bill would have left unfunded; the sponsors, for their part, gained a stated position on abolishing the tax code without having to defend the consequences of actually doing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the existing tax code continued

for.name: Sen. Tim Hutchinson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would terminate the Internal Revenue Code after 2003, and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 20 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, including Sens. Brownback, McCain, Gramm, Domenici, Helms, and Craig.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat is recorded as supporting it; the bill died in committee rather than through a recorded opposition vote.

industries.note: The bill would abolish the income and estate taxes that fall mainly on high earners and large estates, while keeping the payroll taxes that take the biggest share of a working family's paycheck. Its benefits would be sharply tilted toward the top.

industries.industry: Tax preparation, accounting, and tax software industry
industries.note: Terminating the entire Internal Revenue Code would eliminate the compliance work the industry is built on, though any replacement system would eventually generate a new version of that business. Its interest is in keeping some code, not necessarily this one.
The bill declares that the replacement system should eliminate the tax bias against savings and investment, which would favor capital income over wage income if implemented.
